pr_title: Fix EVP_PKEY_eq() to be possible to use with strictly private keys
pr_body:
EVP_PKEY_eq() assumed that an EVP_PKEY always has the public key
component if it has a private key component.  However, this assumption
no longer strictly holds true, at least for provider backed keys.
EVP_PKEY_eq() therefore needs to be modified to specify that the
private key should be checked too (at the discretion of what's
reasonable for the implementation doing the actual comparison).

Fixes #16704
pr_comments: @baentsch, you might want to look at this to see if it makes sense to you, both what `EVP_PKEY_eq()` asks and the example that the mods of our provider KEYMGMT implementations give you.
This pull request is ready to merge

I think this is a great example of a feature that has been changed into a bug.
This function was a replacement for the _cmp function which did NOT operate on private keys. This is changing existing behavior that is documented.

> This function was a replacement for the _cmp function which did NOT operate on private keys

From [the 1.1.1 manual](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man1.1.1/man3/EVP_PKEY_cmp.html):

> **NOTES**
> ...
> Since OpenSSL private keys contain public key components too the function EVP_PKEY_cmp() can also be used to determine if a private key matches a public key.

So it did indeed operate on private keys, from the caller's perspective.  Our decision to drop the assumption that a private key includes the public, this function got its behavior changed implicitly.

> So it did indeed operate on private keys, from the caller's perspective. Our decision to drop the assumption that a private key includes the public, this function got its behavior changed implicitly.

Err.. it did so by just comparing the public key bit.. Not the private key bit??

> Err.. it did so by just comparing the public key bit.. Not the private key bit??

*... from the caller's perspective...*

A caller usually has an EVP_PKEY that they know are a "private key" because it includes the private key bits, or a "public key" because it doesn't.

The simple fact is that what the caller knows as "private key" could be compared with another "private key" in 1.1.1, but cannot necessarily do so any more in 3.0.

> Err.. it did so by just comparing the public key bit.. Not the private key bit??

Arguably unnecessary for legacy keys (as they always contained both public & private key material); the issue was triggered by quantum-safe keys where it's not guaranteed that public key material can be re-generated from private key material (e.g., when loading a private key). The doc update in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/16705/commits/1cf9e849696b2f54c5e453e43546c18d57dbc0eb was key for (my understanding of) this, i.e., what is expected of a provider's key match function. Thus, if the the code update in this PR gets voted down, please retain the doc update. Thanks to @levitte for both.

(A bit offtopic here, don't know a better place to write it down)

IRL we should be able to do at least the following comparisons:

1. Match between a private and public key (ternary, match/not match/unknown)
2. We can check if 2 keys are totally interchangeable (means we have equal parameters and private keys and, either both have equal public keys or both don't have public keys)
3. Match if public keys and parameters are equal (ignoring private keys at all)
4. Match if private keys and parameters are equal (ignoring public keys at all)
5. Match if parameters are equal

IMO, this change is not the right path to take. This puts provider authors on the spot. And potentially breaks existing providers. This forces one to make an arbitrary decision about what selection means in `keymgmt_match()` of a provider. Think of having an unexportable key and we call `SSL_CTX_check_private_key()` to compare the pubkey in a certificate with the opaque private key. That would call `EVP_PKEY_eq()`, the public key gets imported to the external provider, and  its `keymgmt_match()` gets called. 

Earlier this was all good and easy, as selection would be `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY` and we can indeed match those. But with `KEYPAIR` in selection by default, are we supposed to just match what we have access to, or error out because private keys would not match (or could not be compared)? The latter would, however, break `SSL_CTX_check_private_key()`. Just changing the logic in `keymgmt_match()` is not possible without some arbitrary decision making. How should the provider decide whether to match only parameters or public key or private key as `KEYPAIR` implies all of them (or one of them as suggested here). I know the corresponding change in default provider made here could be emulated by all providers. But it looks wrong and is an avoidable regression.

I think one way to fix this would be to keep the current test, and only if it fails try again using `selection = OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECTION_PRIVATE_KEY` -- all done in `EVP_PKEY_eq()`.  Or call `keymgmt_has()` and construct an appropriate `selection`. Do not change the behaviour in default provider as that will have to be mimicked by other providers too.

> are we supposed to just match what we have access to

Yes, that is how I'd understand it: Whichever key part the provider has access to (either public OR private) must match. Therefore I don't think existing providers _must_ be changed: Shouldn't they already handle the "constituent" cases (`OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY | OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY`)? _One_ of them matching should lead to a match decision for `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_KEYPAIR`, no? 
A bit more tricky would be the case where the provider _only_ has access to a private key for one `EVP_PKEY` and the public key for the other `EVP_PKEY`. But a) that doesn't happen with "classic crypto" keypairs and b) there should be a mathematical match operation between the two (or the two keys _really_ don't match).

> Shouldn't they already handle the "constituent" cases (`OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY | OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY`)? _One_ of them matching should lead to a match decision for `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_KEYPAIR`, no? 

If one accepts that approach, the problem this PR is trying to solve is in the default provider, not `EVP_PKEY_eq()`. While holding private keys the former returns false to a match query that uses PUBLIC_KEY as the selection. Instead it could be made match the private keys and conclude whether public keys match or not.  Other providers could handle it as appropriate for their keys.

The selection bits aren't necessarily a precise surgical instrument, so it's true that some decision making is left to the providers.  Providers are expected to do what makes the most sense with it.

However, there is a limitation; provider functions are supposed to make sense of the bits that are *set*, not of the bits that are unset.  The idea that, just because the `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY` is set, providers would start assuming that the `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY` is always involved, violates that limitation.  (if some call passes `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY` and not `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY`, then only the public part should be acted upon, not the private part).

And that's what leaves liboqs dead in the water.  Because we currently only pass `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY` to them, and a public key isn't possible to compute on the fly (*), they face an impossible situation, because there isn't any other function to compare two `EVP_PKEY`s.

-----
(*) Incidently, this came as a bit of a surprise.  The assumption made so far is that any private key comes with a public part, *or* that the public part is possible to compute on the fly (which we do with some key types in 1.1.1, btw)
All this being said, the OTC did discuss this in October...  it's unfortunate that what was said there wasn't reflected here.  It's possible that another round is needed.

>  provider functions are supposed to make sense of the bits that are set, not of the bits that are unset. 

Where is this assumption documented? And is it already adhered to with "classic crypto"? Couldn't one argue that the "classical crypto" assumption (rather capability, i.e., that one can always compute a public key from a private one) is already a violation of this assumption (as one uses --effectively-- a private key to compare a public key)?

In general, if a provider knows about mathematical correlations between those public and private key (parts) that it manages (e.g., a 1:1 relationship, i.e., no private key can belong to another public key than "its own" and vice versa) why shouldn't it be free to operate as it sees fit on bits "not requested" for comparison?

> > provider functions are supposed to make sense of the bits that are set, not of the bits that are unset.
> 
> Where is this assumption documented? And is it already adhered to with "classic crypto"? Couldn't one argue that the "classical crypto" assumption (rather capability, i.e., that one can always compute a public key from a private one) is already a violation of this assumption (as one uses --effectively-- a private key to compare a public key)?
> 
> In general, if a provider knows about mathematical correlations between those public and private key (parts) that it manages (e.g., a 1:1 relationship, i.e., no private key can belong to another public key than "its own" and vice versa) why shouldn't it be free to operate as it sees fit on bits "not requested" for comparison?

This is a perfectly valid point, and in fact, it's already been argued that if a provider *can* compute a public key from its private key data, it's all fine.  So let me rephrase what I said: selectors are an indication of what is desired in cases like this; no one can stop anyone from walking outside that boundary, just be aware that you're then walking in murky waters, and you might not work compatibly with the rest of the eco-system.
OTC: This is good for 3.0.
Needs a test.
Rebased on top of a fresh master

Tests added.  I make a separate branch in my fork with only these tests, and they fail miserably there:
https://github.com/levitte/openssl/tree/extra-evp_extra_test-20211210
This pull request is ready to merge

Merged

issue_context.title: EVP_PKEY_eq() doesn't live up to its promise for provider keys
issue_context.body:
This was identified in another issue: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/16267#issuecomment-928997751

In [EVP_PKEY_eq(3)](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man3.0/man3/EVP_PKEY_eq.html), the following is found:

> **DESCRIPTION**
> ...
> The function EVP_PKEY_eq() checks the public key components and parameters (if present) of keys **a** and **b** for equality.
> ...
> **NOTES**
> ...
> Since OpenSSL private keys contain public key components too the function EVP_PKEY_eq() can also be used to determine if a private key matches a public key.

So for all intents and purposes, was assumed that `EVP_PKEY_eq()` could compare any key, no matter what...

... except we decided that an `EVP_PKEY` doesn't necessarily have to hold a public key, and the assumption that `EVP_PKEY_eq()` can be used to compare private keys via their public key no longer holds.

Do note that for legacy EVP_PKEYs, the ever present public key is still a valid assumption (because existing implementations are built with the older assumption, and the method structure obligates it anyway), so this issue is only about EVP_PKEYs with provider backends.
comments:
Referring to [this comment](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/16267#issuecomment-929976120) and FWIW I completely agree that this text should be made more visible particularly in the context of provider keys: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/398ae8231650c4bd8ddff0e5efd38233c23b1ca0/doc/man7/provider-keymgmt.pod#L203-L208 

The reverse statement (private key equality means public key equality) then also permits the implementation of key matching for OQS keys so far tentatively done: If no public key is present, but `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY` is requested, a private key compare is done instead: https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/blob/6469b466475ea426d637dbbb31b46d88110a7c0c/oqsprov/oqs_kmgmt.c#L130-L137

> If no public key is present, but `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY` is requested, a private key compare is done instead

It might be wise to check that any of `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_KEYPAIR` is present.
This should be closed, shouldn't it?

> This should be closed, shouldn't it?

Yes. But it looks like I don't have permission to do so.

> > This should be closed, shouldn't it?
> 
> Yes. But it looks like I don't have permission to do so.

No problem, I'm doing it.  Now

review_comments: OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_KEYPAIR contains 2 bits, making this if confusing. Can I suggest you replace it with OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY|OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY so it's clear that the if is for either bit.

It acts as a 2-bit mask, yes.

Seriously?
Nitpick: Is this `if` necessary? Doesn't `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_KEYPAIR` _always_ imply `SSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PUBLIC_KEY`? OK, compiler may fix it anyway...

No, as per the decision to allow keys with just the private component.  In other words, it's perfecfly reasonable for someone to use the selector `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_DOMAIN_PARAMETERS | OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY`.  It's not reasonable to do that in `EVP_PKEY_eq()`, but would be reasonable if someone wants to implement something like `EVP_PKEY_priv_eq()` with the expectation that it only works on keys that have a private key component.
Hmm -- I'd agree if the "leading" `if` selector test above were for `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_DOMAIN_PARAMETERS`. But it is `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_KEYPAIR`...
Er, I don't follow your logic...

If you look further down the code, you'll see that domain parameters are checked separately.  Why should the check of the private/public key bits depend on if domain parameters were desired?

See, it's also perfectly reasonable for someone to just use the selector `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_PRIVATE_KEY`

OK, then I misunderstood your statement regarding `OSSL_KEYMGMT_SELECT_DOMAIN_PARAMETERS`. In that case the code just has a superfluous `if` statement -- which a smart compiler probably kills knowing that https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/398ae8231650c4bd8ddff0e5efd38233c23b1ca0/include/openssl/core_dispatch.h#L551-L552 . Sorry for the distraction. Consider my comments resolved then. Thanks again for the update (also regarding documentation).
